newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada-to-Chicago pipe group asks for gas supply.
newsitem.headline: Canada-to-Chicago pipe group asks for gas supply.

text.p: Canada's Alliance Pipeline consortium said it aims to attract natural gas shipping commitments totaling 1.25 billion cubic feet a day before the end of next month in its quest to build a pipeline to Chicago from northern Canada.

The group, which wants to build the C$3.6 billion, 3,000- km line to try to end a crippling scarcity of export capacity to the United States, kicked off its open season on Monday at a gathering of more than 100 senior energy executives.

"While this represents less than 10 percent of the gas supply in western Canada, we are asking producers to consider committing 20 percent of their supply," Alliance spokesman Jack Crawford told a media briefing on Tuesday.
"With their support, Alliance will proceed."
The project, which has been two years in the making, would begin shipping the huge volume of gas by late 1999 under current plans.
A lack of export capacity has often been blamed for Canadian natural gas prices trading well below those in the U.S. Gulf Coast.

The Alliance consortium includes 18 companies, including such producers as Gulf Canada Resources Ltd, Crestar Energy Inc, Ranger Oil and Chevron Corp unit Chevron Canada Resources. Pipeline giant IPL Energy Inc is also an owner.
"I think it's fair to say that 1.25 billion a day is a large volume of gas," Crawford said, adding that Alliance faced a "tall task" in attracting the needed supply by the October 31 deadline.
However, he said there was widespread recognition in the Canadian gas industry that more line space was needed.

The group, which foresees charging producers C$1.14 (US$0.83) to ship a thousand cubic feet of gas the length of the route, said its objective was to allow companies to realize an Empress, Alberta netback of US$0.50 to US$0.55, or about US$0.40 below the NYMEX price.
The current spread is about US$1.
Under the proposal, the 36-inch, high-pressure pipeline would cost C$83 million per year to operate under a planned incentive tariff.
It would also ship ethane in the gas stream to proposed extraction facilities in the Chicago area.
At the briefing, Alliance executives took a softer tone than in the past when discussing NOVA Corp, which currently has a 12 BCFD monopoly on gas shipment in Alberta.
NOVA has disputed Alliance's plans to ship gas past its own system and take gas liquids out of Alberta, where NOVA operates petrochemical plants.
Alliance partners said they hoped deals could be struck with NOVA and Westcoast Energy Inc, British Columbia's gas mover, to allow the interconnection of facilities.

"The Alliance Pipeline is, to some extent, competitive with what NOVA and Westcoast would otherwise do," said Alliance president and chief executive Dennis Cornelson. "But, to some extent, it reinforces the viability of what they do."
Cornelson said that if Alliance and NOVA could work together on projects, costs would be lowered and Canadian gas would be priced more competitively in the Chicago market.
More western Canadian exploration and production would also be stimulated, he said.
"If that happens, then NOVA will be doing a lot more business gathering gas in the province and delivering it to the Alliance system," he said.

The group said it hoped to submit its proposal to the U.S. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission 30 days after the open season if it is successful. It also said it planned to start the approval process with Canada's National Energy Board in mid-1997. -- Reuters Calgary Bureau 403 531-1624
